copyright: The "Body of Knowledge" sculpture by Jaume Plensa at Goethe University in Frankfurt, Germany (© Todamo/Shutterstock)
description: It's World Philosophy Day, when big thinkers gather to discuss life's eternal mysteries. To celebrate, today's image features the 'Body of Knowledge' sculpture at Goethe University in Frankfurt, Germany, which moulds steel letters from eight different alphabets into a human form. Spanish artist Jaume Plensa explains: 'Our body is the home of the spirit. The place in which ideas live.' On World Philosophy Day, we're all encouraged to look beyond easy answers and explore the questions that shape us, and the world around us.

copyright: Pair of barn owls (© Zahoor Salmi/Getty Images)
description: These barn owls, bathed in evening light, are waiting for the hunt to begin. As night falls, these birds of prey swoop into action, listening for tiny movements in grasses or leaves made by mice and voles. Their heart-shaped faces help funnel sound into some of the sharpest ears in the animal kingdom. This allows them to locate their prey with pinpoint precision in the dark before swooping silently, their soft feathers muffling their approach. In autumn, young barn owls strike out to find their own territories. As the nights grow longer, you might spot them earlier in the evening, gliding over fields in search of supper.

copyright: Trail of the Cedars, Glacier National Park, Montana, USA (© DBushue Photography/Getty Images)
description: Today's image features the Trail of the Cedars, one of 1,126 kilometres of hiking trails in Glacier National Park, Montana. Its 1.4-km-long loop includes a raised boardwalk which cuts a path through western red cedars and hemlock trees. The park boasts routes for all abilities, taking in alpine lakes, wildflower meadows, mountain passes and wilderness stretching to the Canadian border.

copyright: Gila Cliff Dwellings National Monument, New Mexico, USA (© Chiara Salvadori/Getty Images)
description: Incredible views and rock-solid foundations are part of the charm of these ancient dwellings, set into the cliffside in New Mexico. Nomads had long used the natural caves above Cliff Dweller Creek as temporary shelter, but it was the Native American Mogollon people who made them their home. Archaeologists believe they created dozens of rooms inside five alcoves in the 1270s and 1280s. Up to 15 families lived here at any one time, raising children, making pottery and overlooking the fertile Gila River valley where they grew crops and hunted wildlife. For reasons unknown, the Mogollon people moved on around 1300, leaving behind one of the American Southwest's most important archaeological sites.

copyright: Frozen azalea with red leaves (© avoferten/Shutterstock)
description: As autumn's first frost sets in, ice crystals form on the leaves of evergreen shrubs, like this azalea. Long gone are the pinks, oranges and yellows of their spring blooms, but a new colourful display awaits, as their green leaves turn shades of red and purple. For the plants, the new pigments protect their leaves as temperatures drop, but for gardeners, they create a vibrant autumnal display, framed in white frost. When spring arrives, new growth will restore the shrub's green leaves and the colourful cycle begins anew.

copyright: Victoria Harbour, Hong Kong, China (© Juan Romero/Cavan Images)
description: Welcome to Hong Kong, home to the world's largest collection of skyscrapers. Those pictured here tower above Victoria Harbour, whose deep waters allowed the island to develop as a busy trading port. Ships carrying tea, silk and other goods have passed through since the 1840s, but growth rocketed in the decades after World War II, fuelling a construction boom. With little flat land available between the harbour and the hills, developers had to build upwards, creating this distinctive skyline. In 2026, Hong Kong has 569 buildings above 150 metres high – more than any other city.

copyright: Sunset over the Damodar River during Chhath Puja (© ParthapratimMukherjee2056/Shutterstock)
description: As the Sun dips towards the horizon, the Damodar River becomes a gathering place for Chhath Puja. The four-day Hindu festival is dedicated to Surya, the Sun God, and Chhathi Maiya. Mainly observed in Bihar, Jharkhand and Uttar Pradesh, as well as parts of Nepal, it is a celebration of gratitude for the Sun and its life-sustaining energy. Devotees observe fasting and gather beside rivers and other bodies of water to pray. One of the festival's most distinctive traditions is offering prayers to both the setting and rising sun, creating striking scenes as families and communities gather at the water's edge at dusk and dawn.
